question: A 36-year-old primigravid woman at 22 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal visit. Her previous prenatal visits showed no abnormalities. She has hyperthyroidism treated with methimazole. She previously smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 15 years but quit 6 years ago. She reports gaining weight after quitting smoking, after which she developed her own weight loss program. She is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) tall and weighs 51.2 kg (112.9 lb); BMI is 18.1 kg/m2. Her temperature is 37°C (98.5°F), pulse is 88/min, and blood pressure is 115/72 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows no abnormalities. The fundus is palpated between the symphysis and the umbilicus. Ultrasound shows a fetal head at the 20th percentile and the abdomen at the 9th percentile. Fetal birth weight is estimated at the 9th percentile and a decreased amniotic fluid index is noted. The maternal quadruple screening test was normal. Thyroid-stimulating hormone is 0.4 mIU/mL, triiodothyronine (T3) is 180 ng/dL, and thyroxine (T4) is 10 μg/dL. Which of the following is the strongest predisposing factor for the ultrasound findings in this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Maternal hyperthyroidism -> Increased metabolic rate -> Increased fetal metabolic demands -> Fetal growth restriction -> Ultrasound findings -> 80% CHAIN: Maternal hyperthyroidism -> Decreased amniotic fluid index -> Ultrasound findings -> 70% CHAIN: Maternal hyperthyroidism -> Altered fetal thyroid hormone levels -> Fetal growth restriction -> Ultrasound findings -> 80%
enhanced_information: Maternal hyperthyroidism can lead to increased fetal metabolic demands and altered fetal thyroid hormone levels, resulting in fetal growth restriction and decreased amniotic fluid index, which are consistent with the ultrasound findings in this patient. The strongest predisposing factor for the ultrasound findings is likely maternal hyperthyroidism.
analysis: Maternal hyperthyroidism can lead to fetal growth restriction and decreased amniotic fluid index due to increased fetal metabolic demands and altered fetal thyroid hormone levels. This aligns with the ultrasound findings in the patient. While other factors like maternal malnutrition or history of tobacco use can impact fetal growth, the enhanced information specifically highlights maternal hyperthyroidism as the strongest predisposing factor in this case.
